---
title: "Pruning"
description: "Reducing a model by removing or zeroing selected weights, neurons, or structures."
term: "Pruning"
letter: "P"
category: "Model Optimization"
difficulty: "Advanced"
---

## Simple explanation

Pruning removes parts of a model that contribute relatively little, aiming
to make it smaller or faster while preserving acceptable quality. It is
similar to trimming a complex structure while keeping its useful behavior.

## Technical explanation

Pruning applies a sparsity pattern to model parameters or structures.
Unstructured pruning zeros individual weights; structured pruning removes
groups such as channels or attention heads. Methods may prune by magnitude,
learned importance, or a task-specific criterion, often followed by
fine-tuning.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Smaller models can reduce storage, memory traffic, and sometimes latency.
Whether pruning yields real deployment benefits depends on hardware and
runtime support: sparse weights do not necessarily execute faster on dense
kernels.

## How it works

A method scores parameters or structures, removes those below a chosen
criterion, and may retrain the remaining model to recover quality. Engineers
measure the resulting quality, memory footprint, and end-to-end inference
performance on the intended hardware.

## Practical example

A team can prune low-magnitude weights from a trained network, fine-tune the
sparse model, and compare its validation accuracy and latency with the
original. If the deployment runtime lacks sparse acceleration, structured
pruning may be more useful.

## Common misconceptions

- A model with many zero weights is not automatically smaller in storage;
  the sparse format itself has overhead.
- Pruning does not guarantee lower latency or energy use without compatible
  hardware and kernels.
